brief: We need a bracket that holds a 4 kg star tracker on a small satellite. It mounts to the side panel and the tracker sits 150 mm out from the panel. Launch is a rideshare; use 15 g quasi-static for design. The tracker needs a stiff mount: tip deflection under load must stay below 1.5 mm. It sits under a solar array hinge, so the plate can be at most 8 mm thick, and there is room for about 80 mm of width. The program uses factors of 1.25 on yield and 1.4 on ultimate.

open_questions: Material and allowable yield and ultimate strengths are not specified; which alloy and temper will be used?
Is the 15 g quasi-static load applied as a single resultant at the tip, and in which axes (lateral, axial, or combined)? Are the three axes to be checked separately?
Is the 150 mm standoff the full cantilever length, or does the bracket have a different effective length including the mounting interface?
Does the 4 kg include the tracker's mounting hardware, and is the bracket's own mass to be counted in the load?
Is a minimum first natural frequency requirement specified for the tracker mount, and does it apply in addition to the 1.5 mm deflection limit?
Are the 1.25 yield and 1.4 ultimate factors to be applied to the 15 g load, and is the 15 g itself already a limit or an ultimate value?
What is the thickness and width direction relative to the load: which dimension governs bending stiffness, and is the 8 mm thickness limit fixed by the solar array hinge clearance?
Are there thermal, misalignment, or star tracker boresight alignment tolerances that impose stricter deflection or angular limits?
What fastener pattern, bolt size, and clamp interface attach the bracket to the side panel, and does the panel itself need a local load check?
Is there a fatigue or vibration environment beyond the quasi-static 15 g case that must be addressed?

reasoning: Worst-case check (load 647.5 N, effective thickness t-0.5 mm, L=150 mm): bending stress sigma = 582714/(b*t^2) MPa must stay below 220.8 MPa (yield) and 221.4 MPa (ultimate) for Al. Deflection requires b*(t-0.5)^3 >= 84580 mm^4 for Al, scaled by E for the others. Among stock thicknesses with 10 <= b <= 80 mm and t/b <= 2, Al 6061-T6 at t=20 mm, b=12 mm gives the smallest cross-section (240 mm^2, about 0.65 kg/m). Ti-6Al-4V at t=20 mm, b=10 mm gives 200 mm^2 but its density (4430) makes it about 0.89 kg/m. Steel 4130 at t=16 mm, b=10 mm gives 160 mm^2 but its density (7850) makes it about 1.26 kg/m, so Al is the lowest-mass feasible choice.

notes.Al 6061-T6: Deflection governs because E=68.9 GPa is low; search t=20 mm with b about 12 mm (needs b*(t-0.5)^3 >= 84580 mm^4, t/b about 1.7), which also satisfies the 220 MPa stress limit and is the lowest-mass candidate at about 240 mm^2.
notes.Ti-6Al-4V: Ultimate stress governs (950/1.4 = 679 MPa, so b*(t-0.5)^2 >= 859 mm^2), and E=113.8 GPa still needs b*(t-0.5)^3 >= 51200 mm^4; try t=20 mm with b=10 mm, which sits exactly at the t/b=2 limit, but its density makes it heavier than Al.
notes.Steel 4130: E=205 GPa makes stiffness easy and yield (435/1.25 = 348 MPa, so b*(t-0.5)^2 >= 1674 mm^2) the driver; try t=16 mm with b=10 mm (160 mm^2), but at 7850 kg/m^3 its mass exceeds the Al and Ti candidates.

text: I'll check the lead's suggested point and a few in-range candidates first. Before running them, I worked the deflection requirement by hand. With the REQ-006 load and thickness, it needs b·(t−0.5)³ ≥ 51,211 mm⁴. Within the 3–8 mm thickness limit and the 80 mm width limit, the largest possible value is 80 × 7.5³ ≈ 33,750 mm⁴, so the in-range designs should all fail.
I'll start with the stiffness-driven candidates. At 8 mm thickness, the REQ-006 deflection limit needs width of about 68 mm, so I'll check widths around that.
The lead's suggested t = 20 mm violates REQ-004, which caps thickness at 8 mm. I'll check the strongest in-range candidate alongside the lead's candidate to confirm.
The 68 mm design passes and the 66 mm design fails REQ-006 (deflection 1.53 mm). I'll check 80 mm to complete the fourth proposal.

The lightest passing Steel 4130 design is 68 mm × 8 mm at about 641 g. Stiffness, not yield, drives the sizing, so the thickness is pinned at the 8 mm maximum.

**Why 8 mm is forced:** REQ-006 (10% higher load, plate 0.5 mm thinner) sets the stiffness limit b·(t−0.5)³ ≥ 28,428 mm³. At t = 6 mm that needs b ≈ 171 mm, outside the 10–80 mm range. At t = 8 mm it needs b ≈ 67.4 mm. Yield is not the lim

**Result: no Al 6061-T6 design can meet all requirements under the current limits. The lead engineer's suggested candidate (t = 20 mm, b = 12 mm) violates REQ-004, which caps thickness at 8 mm.**

**Why it's infeasible:** The tip deflection limit needs I = b·t³/12 ≥ 6,408 mm⁴, so b·t³ ≥ 76,896 mm³. Within the envelope (b ≤ 80 mm, t ≤ 8 mm), the largest possible b·t³ is 80 × 8³ = 40,960 mm³, which

None of the in-range designs pass, and the deflection failure is in the nominal case, not just the robustness case. I'll check the three lightest designs that would pass if the thickness limit were relaxed, so the trade-off is clear.

**No Ti-6Al-4V design meets every requirement.** The thickness limit in REQ-004 (3–8 mm) is what blocks it. Within that range, even the nominal-load tip deflection fails: 80 × 8 mm gives 1.70 mm against the 1.5 mm limit, and it is the stiffest in-range section. The lead's 10 × 20 mm point is the lightest Ti option that passes the structural requirements, but it violates REQ-004 (t = 20 mm).

attacks.title: REQ-006 case: load +10% and plate 0.5 mm thinner
attacks.rationale: Load 647.5 N with a 7.5 mm plate. Survives all strength checks (yield margin 1.284, ultimate 2.141), but tip deflection is 1.486 mm against the 1.5 mm limit, leaving under 1% stiffness margin. 7.5 mm is not a stock thickness, so this case also represents an out-of-spec machining outcome.

attacks.title: Arm lengthened 10 mm after layout change
attacks.rationale: Arm length 160 mm. Deflection scales with L cubed, so it rises to about 1.351 mm, about 21% above the baseline of 1.113 mm. Strength margins stay comfortable (yield 1.68, ultimate 2.686). Survives, but a layout change of this size consumes most of the stiffness headroom.

attacks.title: Width machined 3 mm narrower
attacks.rationale: Width 65 mm. Deflection scales inversely with width, so it rises to about 1.165 mm. Strength margins are yield 1.733 and ultimate 2.758. Survives with reasonable margin, but it shows that the section width is a sensitive parameter for stiffness.

attacks.title: Launch-type load 1.5x
attacks.rationale: A 1.5x load (883 N) keeps yield margin positive at 0.906 and ultimate at 1.621, but tip deflection reaches about 1.67 mm, breaking REQ-003. Stiffness, not strength, is the first requirement to fail. The 1.5x factor is an assumed launch-environment multiplier and should be confirmed against the actual launch environment.

attacks.title: Combined worst case: load +10%, plate 1 mm thinner (7 mm), arm +10 mm, width -3 mm
attacks.rationale: Several realistic changes stacked together. The 7 mm plate is a non-stock thickness from machining or corrosion loss. Yield margin stays positive at 0.783 and ultimate at 1.452, but tip deflection reaches about 2.32 mm against the 1.5 mm limit, failing REQ-003 and REQ-006. Deflection is the failing criterion; the design is strength-adequate but not stiffness-adequate under combined changes.

attacks.title: Fatigue at root fillet and bolt holes under launch vibration and thermal cycling
attacks.rationale: Cyclic loading at the clamp root and bolt holes is not modelled. The static model has no stress concentration factor, no cycle count, and no S-N data for 4130 at these stress levels. Could fail well below the static margins reported.

summary: The 68 x 8 mm Steel 4130 bracket shows pass results for strength, ultimate, worst-case margin, tip deflection, factors of safety, lateral stability proxy, stress corrosion, outgassing, plate availability, buy-to-fly and thickness tolerance, with statuses left unchanged as the engine reported them. Several action items remain open, mainly typical-value allowables, unanalyzed fatigue, unclassified fracture control, corrosion finish, and specialty-metal and traceability requirements before release.
top_risks: M-01: Design allowables are typical handbook values, not MMPDS A- or B-basis values for this alloy, temper and thickness, so the passing margins (S-01 to S-03) rest on unverified inputs.
X-02: Fatigue is not analyzed, and no cyclic load cases such as launch vibration have been evaluated, leaving a gap in the structural case.
M-04 and M-05: 4130 has no corrosion protection specified and the joint has an unresolved dissimilar-metal galvanic risk, which could degrade the bracket in service.

actions.action: Replace the typical handbook values with MMPDS A- or B-basis allowables for Steel 4130, the specified temper and the 8 mm thickness, then re-run S-01 to S-03.
Define the cyclic load cases, including launch vibration, and perform a fatigue analysis before the design review.
Classify the part (for example non-fracture-critical) and record the rationale in the program file.
Specify a plating or primer and paint system per the program finish spec to protect the 4130 surface.
Confirm the specialty metal melt origin (US or qualifying country) under DFARS 252.225-7009 with the vendor before award.

memo: We recommend awarding the order for 10 Steel 4130 brackets to Vendor B (sample), which was selected by the scoring that weighted price at 0.6 and lead time at 0.4. Vendor B bid at $104.39 each with a 13-day lead time, which beat Vendor A's bid of $133.98 each with an 18-day lead time, and both were eligible with no flags. Vendor C was not chosen because it did not bid and was ineligible for lacking an AS9100 quality system, and Vendor D was not chosen because it did not bid and could not certify a DFARS compliant melt source.
